summary: An experimental document that describes NewReno, a specific algorithm for responding to partial acknowledgments during TCP's fast recovery. It was replaced by RFC 3782.

plainLanguage.summary: When several messages get lost in a row, this lets the sender fix them one at a time, instead of giving up early and slowing way down.

questions: how does newreno handle multiple packet losses
when should i use newreno instead of sack
subtitle: How to recover when multiple TCP packets are lost at once.

tldr.problem: When multiple packets are lost during a single network exchange, standard TCP Reno's fast recovery algorithm only retransmits one packet at a time, which is slow. Without detailed loss information, the sender does not know which packets were lost.
tldr.mechanism: NewReno modifies TCP's fast recovery to detect and respond to partial acknowledgments—ACKs that confirm some but not all of the lost packets. When it receives a partial ACK, it immediately retransmits the next lost packet instead of waiting for a timeout.
tldr.outcome: NewReno recovers faster from windows with multiple packet losses when SACK is unavailable, improving throughput in congested networks. However, it was superseded by RFC 3782 as TCP implementations adopted SACK and other improvements.

today: RFC 2582 is an Experimental specification that was obsoleted by RFC 3782. Modern TCP implementations typically use SACK instead of NewReno for more efficient recovery, but NewReno remains relevant for constrained systems and as a fallback algorithm.

sections.title: The Problem with Multiple Losses
sections.content:
TCP uses two mechanisms to recover from packet loss: retransmit timeouts (which are slow) and fast retransmit (which is triggered by three duplicate acknowledgments). When the fast retransmit algorithm activates, the sender retransmits one packet and enters fast recovery to continue sending new data.

The problem arises when multiple packets are lost from the same window of data. After the sender retransmits the first lost packet, it may receive additional duplicate acknowledgments as the receiver confirms other data that was already in flight. These duplicates indicate there may be more losses, but the standard Reno algorithm does not handle this well—it simply waits, hoping that a single retransmission will fix the problem. If additional packets were lost, the sender must eventually wait for a timeout before recovering them all.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine sending a stack of postcards through the mail, and three get lost. The mail carrier tells you three postcards are missing, so you resend the first one. But if six were actually lost, the carrier keeps saying postcards are missing. Reno just waits and hopes; NewReno figures out faster that more are missing.

sections.title: What a Partial Acknowledgment Means
sections.content:
When the sender retransmits a lost packet and continues into fast recovery, it eventually receives an acknowledgment for that retransmitted packet. If only one packet was lost, this ACK will acknowledge all data that was outstanding when fast recovery started. But if multiple packets were lost, this ACK will acknowledge only some of that data—a partial acknowledgment.

The key insight of NewReno is this: a partial acknowledgment is a signal. It means the first retransmitted packet was received, but data beyond it is still missing. The sender should immediately infer that the next packet has been lost and retransmit it, rather than waiting idly or for a timeout.
sections.plainLanguage: When a postcard you resent comes back confirmed, but not all the postcards you sent before, you know some others are still missing. That is a partial confirmation.

sections.title: The NewReno Fast Recovery Algorithm
sections.content:
NewReno modifies standard fast recovery in five steps. When three duplicate ACKs arrive, the sender records the highest sequence number it has sent (called recover) and sets the congestion window. It retransmits the lost packet and enters fast recovery.

For each additional duplicate ACK in fast recovery, it increments the congestion window to reflect data leaving the network. When a new ACK arrives that acknowledges all data up to and including the recover value, fast recovery is complete and the window is deflated to a safe size.

Critically, if the ACK does not reach recover, it is a partial ACK. NewReno responds by immediately retransmitting the next unacknowledged packet, deflating the window by the new data acknowledged, and staying in fast recovery. This loop repeats until all lost packets are recovered.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender keeps a mental note of the highest postcard number sent. If an ACK comes back saying it got everything up to that number, recovery is done. If not, the sender knows more are lost and retransmits the next one right away.

sections.title: Variants and Trade-offs
sections.content:
The RFC documents two variants of how to handle the retransmit timer during recovery. The Impatient variant resets the timer only after the first partial ACK, letting it expire for subsequent losses. The Slow-but-Steady variant resets the timer after each partial ACK, ensuring steady retransmission at one packet per round-trip time when many losses occur.

The document also addresses avoiding false fast retransmits after timeouts. Using a variable called send_high, the sender can distinguish between duplicate ACKs indicating new losses and those caused by its own unnecessary retransmissions, preventing the algorithm from entering fast recovery incorrectly.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two philosophies: the sender can be impatient and eventually time out, or steady and careful, resending one at a time. Each has trade-offs.

sections.title: Limitations and When to Use Alternatives
sections.content:
NewReno is designed for TCP connections without the SACK (Selective Acknowledgement) option. With SACK, the receiver can tell the sender exactly which packets were received and which are missing, making NewReno unnecessary. The RFC recommends that TCP implementations support SACK whenever possible, as it provides much better recovery from multiple losses.

For implementations without SACK, NewReno is recommended over standard Reno. The RFC also notes that the receiver should send immediate ACKs for out-of-order data to help the sender detect losses faster. Simulations are provided in the NS network simulator to validate the algorithm's behavior under various loss scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: If both sides of the connection can talk more precisely (SACK), use that instead—it is much better. NewReno is a fallback for when they cannot.
